title: Satyavati
hook: with the Kuru line about to end, Satyavati asks Bhishma to break his vow, and he refuses her
carry: I will not give up truth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati's house: three princesses carried from Kashi, Amba set free — she had already chosen — and a young king dead without a son. What true thing did you say? Day seven hundred twenty.

A family line is a thin thread. Satyavati has watched hers fray to almost nothing. Her husband is gone. Both of her sons by him are gone. Two young widows grieve in the palace. And the only grown man of the house is Bhishma, who swore, years ago, so that her sons would rule, never to take the throne and never to father children. Now she calls him to her. And the woman his vow was made for is about to ask him to break it.
screen: `A HUSBAND, TWO SONS, GONE.` → `ONE MAN LEFT.` → `SHE CALLS HIM IN.`

segments.voice: Satyavati makes her case carefully, the way someone does who has thought about it at night. The offerings to the ancestors, the name of Shantanu, the whole house, she says, now rest on you. You know what dharma asks. So do this: take the throne, and raise children with your brother's widows, so the line goes on. She isn't asking lightly. In the world of the poem, a line with no sons means no one to make the offerings for the dead. But Bhishma says no. He reminds her of what he swore, and why: so that her children would rule. And then he says something like this: he could give up the three worlds, the kingdom of the gods, anything greater than that, but he will not give up truth. The earth could lose its scent, water its wetness, the sun its glory, before he breaks his word. Hear how strange that is. The very vow that made her a queen is now the thing standing between her and an heir. Her father's condition drew that vow out once. Now she asks for it back, and it won't come back. Some readers see Bhishma's refusal as the poem's picture of keeping one's word at any cost. Some see it as the first sign that his vow will cost his family dearly. The text gives both of them room. Satyavati asks once more, for the need of the moment, and he still holds. But there's one thing she hasn't told anyone yet, and tomorrow she tells it.
screen: `THE ANCESTORS' OFFERINGS.` · `TAKE THE THRONE, SHE ASKS.` · `I WILL NOT GIVE UP TRUTH.` · `THE VOW THAT MADE HER QUEEN.`

segments.voice: Settle in and let the breath find its own length. Bhishma's word held, even when the person it served asked him to drop it. Bring to mind one promise you're still keeping. It might be small: a weekly call, a debt, a habit you swore to. Hold it in mind without deciding anything about it. Ask it quietly: who is this still for? Breathe in on the promise. Breathe out on the people it touches. The bell holds the time.
Satyavati. The queen who asks Bhishma to break the vow that made her queen, and hears him refuse.
Your line: I will not give up truth. Today, look at one promise you keep and ask who it's still for. Day seven hundred twenty.

howItsDone: In Hindu tradition, offerings to the ancestors are called shraddha, and some families keep the season called Pitru Paksha for them; the worry in this story is that no one will be left to make them.

fork.setup: you're Bhishma. the queen your vow was made for asks you to break it. what do you do?
options: break it, for the family's sake.
fork.reveal: he refuses: the earth could lose its scent before he gave up his word.

original.note: Sanskrit satya: truth, the thing Bhishma says he will never give up.

trapdoor: what you thought: a stubborn man saying no.
what it means: a vow made for Satyavati now blocking what she needs.
what a scholar hears: Bhishma's refusal lists what nature might give up before he would give up truth.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Satyavati asks Bhishma to raise offspring and take the throne; Bhishma's refusal)

notes: All paraphrase, including Bhishma's speech (the three worlds; earth giving up its scent, water its moisture, the sun its light). Confirm the list in Ganguli; it was not quoted because the exact wording was not certain.
Satyavati's appeal to the ancestors' offerings and Shantanu's line is paraphrased; confirm.
The two readings of Bhishma's refusal are unattributed and unranked.
The original-language item gives the plain meaning of satya and makes no claim linking it to Satyavati's name.
howItsDone names shraddha and Pitru Paksha; confirm phrasing.

Editor pass: in Ganguli Satyavati presses Bhishma a second time, so 'doesn't argue further' and the matching myth item were corrected; 'the sun its light' changed to 'glory' to match the text's list; the vow is no longer said to be sworn 'for her sake' or asked for by her father (he set the condition; the celibacy vow answered it); howItsDone generalization softened.
